items.name: ch5_6
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices funny cartoon characters (a cheeky time-traveller, khans, princes, tsars, servants, nobles, officers, an empress): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags.
lines: Peter was born in sixteen seventy-two.
At ten, he became co-tsar with his half-brother, while his older sister Sophia actually ran things.
That same year, rebel palace guards, the Streltsy, stormed the Kremlin, and young Peter watched them kill members of his mother's family in front of him.
Peter grew up outside the palace, playing war games with real soldiers and real cannons. He grew to over two metres tall. Around six foot eight.
[looking up, way up] He had to duck through most doorways in Russia.
In sixteen ninety-seven, he did something no tsar had ever done. He went to Western Europe himself, in disguise, as "Peter Mikhailov".
He worked as a carpenter in Dutch shipyards, studied English factories, and fell in love with everything modern.
You're seven feet tall and fifty men follow you everywhere.
Back home, he started changing Russia by force. He ordered his nobles to shave their beards. He cut some off himself, with scissors.
If you really wanted to keep your beard, you paid a beard tax, and carried a token to prove it.
[stroking his chin] Imagine needing a licence for your face.
European clothes. A new calendar, with New Year on January the first. Schools for maths and navigation. A real navy.
He fought Sweden for twenty-one years. He lost badly at Narva in seventeen hundred... then smashed the Swedes at Poltava in seventeen oh nine.
Now Russia had what it always wanted: a way to the Baltic Sea.
And on a swamp by that sea, Peter built a brand new capital: Saint Petersburg. Thousands of forced labourers died building it.
He made himself Emperor. Russia was now an empire.
But Peter's total control reached his own family. His son Alexei hated the reforms and fled abroad.
Peter lured him home with promises, then had him put on trial. Alexei died in prison in seventeen eighteen.
[quietly] That's the second tsar in this story to lose his son by his own hand.
Peter then made a new law: the emperor could pick any heir he liked. And in seventeen twenty-five, he died... without picking anyone.
For the next thirty-seven years, Russia had a strange system: whoever the palace guards liked, became ruler.
Empresses, a child emperor, regents: one palace coup after another.
In seventeen forty-four, a teenage German princess named Sophie arrived in Russia to marry the heir to the throne, Peter.
She learned Russian. She converted to Orthodoxy. She took a new name: Catherine.
Her husband, meanwhile, preferred playing with toy soldiers and openly worshipped Russia's enemy, the King of Prussia.
In seventeen sixty-two, he became Peter the Third, and immediately handed back everything Russia had won from Prussia in a long, bloody war.
[stunned] He won the game, then gave the other team the trophy.
Your Majesty, the guards are... unhappy with your husband.
[standing, smiling] Then I suppose I should get dressed.
Six months into his reign, Catherine and the guards overthrew him. A week later, Peter was dead. The official cause, the story goes, was a "stomach problem".

Catherine the Second ruled for thirty-four years. She wrote to famous French thinkers like Voltaire, collected thousands of paintings, which became the Hermitage museum, and talked about freedom and reason.
She also grabbed a lot of land. Crimea in seventeen eighty-three. Big parts of Poland, which was carved up until it disappeared from the map.
And her traders crossed the Pacific. In seventeen eighty-four, Russians built their first permanent settlement in a faraway place called... Alaska.
[checking his watch, grinning] Ooh. Remember that one. We know how this ends.
But for most Russians, life got harder. Millions of peasants were serfs, owned by landlords, bought and sold with the land.
In seventeen seventy-three, a Cossack called Pugachev claimed to be the dead Peter the Third, and led a huge peasant uprising across the Volga. It took two years to crush.
Freedom for the nobles, control for everyone else. The loop, in a powdered wig.
[to camera] By the way, if you're enjoying this, subscribe. It's free, and it makes the time machine run.
When Catherine died in seventeen ninety-six, Russia was a giant on Europe's stage.
And in the west, a short French general was about to test exactly how big that giant really was.
